prompt.context: Our client is A+ Airline Co., the third largest airline in the United States by passengers carried. This week, we have been flying on our primary competitor, Gamma Airline, and we noticed something interesting: they stopped accepting cash for in-flight food and beverage services and they now only accept major credit cards.
prompt.question: The CEO of A+ Airline Co. wants to know: why did Gamma Airline switch from a Cash & Card system to a credit card only system, and should we follow them?

clarifying_info.q: What percentage of passengers have a credit card available?
clarifying_info.a: Roughly 99% of all consumers purchase their airline tickets using a credit card, so essentially all consumers on an airplane have a credit card available to them.

clarifying_info.q: What items are sold on A+ Airline flights?
clarifying_info.a: Only food and alcoholic beverage items are sold on A+ Airline flights.

clarifying_info.q: Does this decision apply to international flights?
clarifying_info.a: This is a US domestic decision only. Ignore international.

clarifying_info.q: Has any other airline made the switch besides Gamma?
clarifying_info.a: Gamma is the only airline that has made the switch so far; however, all other airlines are evaluating the switch.

clarifying_info.q: How similar are Gamma and A+ Airline?
clarifying_info.a: For the purposes of this case, Gamma and A+ Airline should be considered to be exactly the same in all regards.

exhibits.title: An Average A+ Airline Flight
exhibits.shows: Seat configuration, load factors, purchase rates, average spend, and current cash vs. card payment split for an average A+ Airline Boeing 737-800 flight

first_class.note: First Class passengers receive free food & beverage

exhibits.title: A+ Airline Cash & Card Operations
exhibits.shows: Side-by-side process flows for the current Cash Management process (8 steps, 31 days total time, 2% fee, 5 cash handlers + 2 processing center employees per airport, $50 change loaded per flight) and the Credit Card process (3 steps, 24 hours total time, 2% fee)

data.cash_staff: 5 cash handlers per airport + 2 employees in onsite cash processing center per airport

framework: Revenue Changes: Loss of cash-only customers who will not convert to card vs. any increase in card-using customers
Cost Changes: Benefit of eliminating cash management overhead costs vs. incremental credit card processing fees
Cash Flow & TVM Changes: Faster payment collection (credit card settles in 24 hours vs. 31 days for cash), time value of money benefits, and working capital improvement

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the total market size in dollars for food and beverage purchases on an average flight, and determine the current split between cash and card spending.
questions.guidance: Interviewee should work through seat counts, apply load factors, split by traveler type, apply purchase rates and average spend, then apply the 20%/80% cash/card split. No rounding allowed.

math.setup: Step 1: Passenger counts. First Class: 200 * 25% = 50 seats, 100% load = 50 passengers, all business travelers. Economy: 200 * 75% = 150 seats, 80% load = 120 passengers, 50% business = 60, 50% leisure = 60. Total: 170 passengers (50 FC + 60 Econ Business + 60 Econ Leisure). Note: FC gets free food so only Economy passengers are counted for purchases: 60 business + 60 leisure = 120 economy passengers. Step 2: Purchasers. Business (economy): 60 * 75% = 45 purchasers at $10 = $450. Leisure (economy): 60 * 25% = 15 purchasers at $5 = $75. Total: 60 purchasers, $525 total spend. Step 3: Cash vs. Card split. Cash: 20% * $525 = $105. Card: 80% * $525 = $420.
steps: First Class passengers: 50 * 100% = 50 (all business, free food - excluded from purchase calc)
math.answer: Total in-flight food & beverage revenue per flight: $525. Cash purchases: $105 (20%). Card purchases: $420 (80%).

questions.prompt: We will lose 1/3 of current cash customers when we switch to card-only. Calculate the revenue impact of losing those customers.
questions.guidance: Interviewee should apply the 1/3 loss rate to cash purchasers (not cash spend directly), then compute lost revenue by traveler segment. The result is a $35 revenue loss per flight.

math.setup: Cash purchasers by segment: Business cash purchasers = 1/3 of cash spend attributable to business. Cash spend = $105 total. Business share: 45 purchasers / 60 total = 75% of purchasers, so business cash = $105 * (45/60) = $78.75 → but simpler approach: identify # of cash purchasers then lose 1/3. Total cash purchasers: 60 * 20% = 12 (or use spend/avg spend). Business cash customers: 45 * 20% = 9; lose 1/3 = 3 customers, loss = 3 * $10 = $30. Leisure cash customers: 15 * 20% = 3; lose 1/3 = 1 customer, loss = 1 * $5 = $5. Total loss: $35. New total revenue: $525 - $35 = $490.
math.answer: Revenue loss of $35 per flight (3 business + 1 leisure customer lost). New revenue: $490/flight.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, analyze the cost changes from switching to card-only. What are the cost savings and any new costs?
questions.guidance: Interviewee should identify: (1) the 2% processing fee exists under BOTH systems, so it is a wash; (2) cash management overhead (7 employees per airport) can be eliminated, saving $35/flight; (3) the $50 change loaded per flight ties up working capital. The net cost saving is $35/flight.

math.setup: Credit card fee: 2% on all transactions - this already exists for card payments and would apply to all transactions under card-only. Cash management also has a 2% fee. These offset - no net change in fees. Overhead savings: 7 employees per airport (5 cash handlers + 2 processing center) are eliminated. Total per-flight savings from eliminating cash management overhead = $35/flight (given by interviewer when asked).
steps: Cash management fee: 2% on cash collected
Credit card fee: 2% on card transactions
Fee comparison: both 2% - this is a wash, no net change
Cash overhead: 5 cash handlers + 2 processing center employees = 7 employees per airport eliminated
Working capital: $50 change per flight freed up
math.answer: Net cost saving: $35/flight from eliminating cash management overhead. Credit card fees are a wash (both processes charge 2%). Additionally, $50 per flight in change is freed up.

questions.prompt: Qualitatively, what is the impact of receiving payment 30 days sooner under a card-only system?
questions.guidance: Interviewee should identify Time Value of Money benefits and working capital improvements without needing to calculate a precise NPV number.

brainstorming.prompt: What qualitative benefits and risks should A+ Airline consider when evaluating this switch?

categories.name: Time Value of Money & Cash Flow
ideas: Receive payment 30 days sooner (24 hours vs. 31 days)
Money can be invested in interest-earning accounts
Can pay down lines of credit faster
Can pay suppliers early to capture early-payment discounts

categories.name: Working Capital
ideas: Eliminate $50 in change loaded per flight, freeing up cash
Reduction in cash loss due to theft
Reduction in cash loss due to damaged bills
No need to maintain onsite cash processing infrastructure

categories.name: Customer Experience
ideas: Faster transaction speed improves customer satisfaction
Passengers less likely to abandon a purchase due to long wait times for change
Proven psychological effect: card-only eliminates guilt around using a card, increasing average spend
Economy passengers at the back of the plane benefit most from faster service

categories.name: Operational Simplicity
ideas: Eliminates 8-step cash management process
Reduces coordination with armored car services
Fewer staff required at airports
Lower risk of cash handling errors

categories.name: Risks & Costs
ideas: WiFi/connectivity cost to process card transactions in-flight
Increased fraud risk with card-only implementation
Potential negative PR from cash-preferring customers
Regulatory considerations for cash acceptance
System downtime risk - if card terminals fail, no sales possible

recommendation: A+ Airline should switch to a credit card only system for in-flight food and beverage purchases

The quantitative case is break-even: $35 revenue loss from lost cash customers is exactly offset by $35 in overhead savings - but the savings are to the bottom line while the revenue loss is top-line, making the switch net positive on profit
The qualitative case strongly supports the switch: faster payment collection, improved working capital, better customer experience, and reduced operational complexity
risks: Loss of cash-preferring customers who refuse to use cards (estimated 1/3 of current cash users, ~4 passengers per flight)
Technology risk: card terminal failures could result in zero in-flight sales
Potential fraud increase with card-only system
WiFi connectivity costs to verify transactions in-flight
next_steps: Pilot the card-only system on select routes to validate assumptions about customer loss rates and purchase behavior
Evaluate card terminal reliability and establish backup procedures
Analyze connectivity infrastructure costs for in-flight card processing
Monitor Gamma Airline's results post-switch for benchmarking
Develop communication plan for passengers explaining the policy change
